name: Kubernetes
tagline: Pods, scheduling, autoscaling and a real Kind cluster.
headline: Kubernetes,
animated.
blurb: Every core concept as an animated diagram, with real-life analogies, YAML from basic to advanced, a scheduler simulator that explains why a pod lands where it does, and a real Kind cluster playground with guided labs.

beginner.what: Kubernetes runs containerized applications across a group of machines. You describe the state you want, and Kubernetes keeps working to make the running system match it.
beginner.why: It helps teams deploy and scale many services consistently, recover from failed containers, and manage changes without hand-operating every machine.
beginner.example: Think of a restaurant manager who keeps enough cooks on shift. If one is absent or orders increase, the manager adjusts staffing; Kubernetes does similar work for application copies.
beginner.start: Begin with a Pod, then learn how Deployments keep the desired number of copies running and Services give them a stable address.

name: Databases
tagline: SQL, indexes, transactions, isolation and scaling data.
headline: Databases,
demystified.
blurb: From your first SELECT to MVCC, isolation anomalies, query plans and sharding. Run real SQL against a seeded shop database and watch two transactions race each other.

beginner.what: A database stores information so applications can find it, change it, and keep it consistent over time. Relational databases organize much of that information into tables and relationships.
beginner.why: Applications need dependable memory: customer records, orders, settings, and events must survive restarts and remain correct when many people use the system at once.
beginner.example: An online shop stores customers, products, and orders. A transaction makes sure an order and its payment record are saved together or neither is saved.
beginner.start: Start with tables, rows, keys, and a simple SELECT query before moving on to indexes and transactions.

name: System Design
tagline: Scale, caching, queues, consistency and interview case studies.
headline: System design,
visualised.
blurb: Load balancers, caches, queues, consistent hashing and CAP, each as a moving diagram. Stress-test an architecture with live traffic and do back-of-the-envelope maths like in a real interview.

beginner.what: System design is the process of deciding how software components, data, and infrastructure fit together to meet a product's needs.
beginner.why: A feature that works for one user may fail under millions of requests, regional outages, or slow dependencies. Design makes those tradeoffs visible before they become expensive incidents.
beginner.example: For a photo-sharing app, decide how users upload images, where images are stored, how feeds are built, and what happens when a storage service is unavailable.
beginner.start: Begin with requirements and traffic estimates. Then draw the simplest request path before choosing databases, caches, queues, or multiple services.

name: Git
tagline: Commits, branches, merge vs rebase, undoing and internals.
headline: Git,
untangled.
blurb: See the commit graph move as you type git commands. Merge, rebase, reset, revert and cherry-pick in a safe simulator, then solve challenges that mirror real team workflows.

beginner.what: Git records changes to files as a history of commits. It lets people work on separate branches and combine their changes later.
beginner.why: Teams need to review work, understand what changed, coordinate safely, and recover an earlier version without keeping piles of copied folders.
beginner.example: A branch is like a draft copy of a document. You can experiment there, review the changes, and merge them into the shared version when ready.
beginner.start: Learn the working tree, staging area, and commit first; then practice branches, merges, and undoing a change safely.

name: Python
tagline: Objects, functions, generators, async and the GIL.
headline: Python,
step by step.
blurb: Names and objects, closures, decorators, generators, asyncio and the GIL. Step through real code line by line and watch every variable and stack frame change.

beginner.what: Python is a general-purpose programming language used to automate tasks, build applications, analyze data, and connect services.
beginner.why: Its readable syntax lets people express useful work with relatively little code, making it common for scripting, APIs, data work, and prototypes.
beginner.example: A short script can read a CSV file, calculate totals, and write a report that would otherwise take repeated manual steps.
beginner.start: Begin with values, variables, conditions, loops, and functions. Run small examples and inspect how each value changes.

name: AWS
tagline: IAM, VPC, compute, storage, serverless and architecture.
headline: AWS,
without the bill.
blurb: Regions, IAM, VPCs, EC2, S3, Lambda and friends, explained with flows. Evaluate IAM policies like AWS does and debug VPC reachability without spending a cent.

beginner.what: AWS is a cloud platform that provides computing, storage, networking, databases, identity, and other services on demand.
beginner.why: Organizations can provision resources when needed and design for growth or failure without buying and operating every server themselves.
beginner.example: A web application can run on compute instances, store images in object storage, and use an identity policy to control which service can access them.
beginner.start: Learn regions and accounts, then understand IAM permissions and the basic network path before deploying compute.

name: Linux
tagline: Files, permissions, pipes, processes, systemd and the kernel.
headline: Linux,
from the shell up.
blurb: The filesystem, permissions, pipes, text tools, processes, systemd, networking and what containers really are. Practise in a simulated shell with real files, users and services, and solve hands-on challenges.

beginner.what: Linux is an operating system used on servers, cloud machines, containers, and many devices. Its shell provides commands to inspect and manage the system.
beginner.why: Knowing Linux helps engineers understand where applications run, diagnose resource and permission problems, and automate repeatable operations.
beginner.example: When a service cannot write a file, check the path, owner, permissions, process identity, and available disk space from the shell.
beginner.start: Begin with files and directories, then practice reading command output, permissions, processes, and pipes.

name: Java
tagline: JVM, collections, streams, records, virtual threads and GC.
headline: Java,
from 8 to 25.
blurb: From the JVM and collections to records, pattern matching, virtual threads and garbage collectors. Compare the same code across Java 8, 11, 14, 17, 18, 21 and 25 side by side, and check the minimum version any snippet needs.

beginner.what: Java is a programming language whose programs typically run on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which manages execution across supported platforms.
beginner.why: It is widely used for long-running backend services and business applications, where predictable tooling, libraries, and runtime behavior matter.
beginner.example: A Java service can accept a web request, validate it, call a database, and return a response while the JVM manages memory and threads.
beginner.start: Learn classes, objects, methods, and collections before studying the JVM, garbage collection, and concurrency.

name: CI/CD
tagline: Pipelines, tests, artifacts, deployments and safe rollbacks.
headline: CI/CD,
shipped safely.
blurb: From the first commit hook to blue-green and canary releases. Watch a pipeline run stage by stage, break it with flaky tests and slow builds, then fix it with caching, parallelism and automatic rollbacks.

beginner.what: CI/CD automates the steps that take a code change from a developer's commit through checks, packaging, and delivery or deployment.
beginner.why: Automation makes releases repeatable, catches problems earlier, and gives teams a safer way to ship changes frequently.
beginner.example: A pipeline can run tests on a pull request, build one versioned artifact, and deploy that same artifact to staging before production.
beginner.start: Start with a pipeline that checks out code, runs one test, and reports a clear pass or failure. Add packaging and deployment after that works.

name: DSA
tagline: Big-O, data structures, sorting, graphs, DP and interview patterns.
headline: Algorithms,
in motion.
blurb: Arrays to graphs, every classic sorting algorithm, recursion, dynamic programming and the patterns interviewers love. Watch sorts race bar by bar and run your own solutions in Python.

beginner.what: Data structures organize information, and algorithms describe the steps used to process it. Together they are often called DSA.
beginner.why: The choice of structure or algorithm affects how much time and memory a program needs as its input grows.
beginner.example: A set can check whether an item was seen quickly, while a list is useful when order and repeated values matter.
beginner.start: Learn arrays, maps, and stacks, then compare simple search and sort methods while counting their operations.

name: QA & Testing
tagline: Test design, automation, the test pyramid, flaky tests and quality.
headline: Quality,
by design.
blurb: Unit, integration and end-to-end tests, test design techniques, mocks, flaky tests and quality metrics. Pick test inputs and watch branch coverage and mutation score change, then run real unittest suites.

beginner.what: Quality assurance and software testing check whether a product behaves as intended and make failures easier to catch before release.
beginner.why: Tests reduce the cost of change by finding regressions, clarify expected behavior, and give teams evidence about release risk.
beginner.example: A checkout test can verify that a valid payment creates one order, while a declined payment does not create a completed order.
beginner.start: Begin by writing expected behavior for one small feature, including a normal case, an invalid input, and a failure from a dependency.

name: Data Science
tagline: Statistics, data wrangling, visualisation and experiments.
headline: Data science,
made visible.
blurb: Descriptive stats, distributions, hypothesis tests, A/B experiments, cleaning and feature engineering. Drag points to see mean, median and correlation move, and analyse data in a Python notebook.

beginner.what: Data science uses data, statistics, and computation to answer questions, find patterns, and support decisions.
beginner.why: It helps turn raw records into evidence while making uncertainty, bias, and data quality visible to decision makers.
beginner.example: A team can compare customer retention across cohorts to learn when users stop returning and which changes may be associated with that pattern.
beginner.start: Ask a specific question, inspect a small dataset, check missing or unusual values, and summarize it before building a model.

name: ML & AI
tagline: Models, training, LLMs, RAG, agents, AGENTS.md and skills.
headline: ML & AI,
neurons to agents.
blurb: Regression to transformers, training and evaluation, LLMs, prompting, RAG, tool calling and AI agents, including how to write AGENTS.md and SKILL.md files. Train a model live and lint your own agent instructions.

beginner.what: Machine learning trains a model from examples so it can make predictions or generate outputs for new inputs.
beginner.why: Some tasks are difficult to describe with fixed rules but have enough examples to learn useful patterns, such as ranking or classification.
beginner.example: A model can learn from labeled messages to estimate whether a new message is spam, then be checked for mistakes and uneven performance.
beginner.start: Begin with a clear prediction goal, a small dataset, a simple baseline, and separate data for evaluation.

name: Security
tagline: Identity, application security, cloud controls and incident response.
headline: Security,
built in.
blurb: Learn threat modeling, authentication, authorization, secure coding, cloud identity and incident response. Use the IAM troubleshooting simulator to trace cross-account access failures one policy layer at a time.

beginner.what: Security protects systems and information from misuse, exposure, tampering, and interruption.
beginner.why: Every application has valuable data and capabilities. Security reduces the chance that an attacker or mistake can cross a boundary and cause harm.
beginner.example: A service should verify who is calling, allow only the actions that identity needs, and record enough evidence to investigate suspicious access.
beginner.start: Identify important assets and trust boundaries, then learn authentication, authorization, input validation, and secret handling.

name: Networking
tagline: IP addressing, CIDR math, routing, DNS, protocols and cloud networks.
headline: Networking,
made calculable.
blurb: Build intuition for IPv4 and IPv6, masks, prefixes such as /24, /32 and /64, subnet ranges, routing, DNS, TCP, TLS, NAT and cloud networking. Calculate the ranges yourself in the interactive CIDR simulator.

beginner.what: Networking moves data between devices and services using addresses, routes, protocols, and rules that control traffic.
beginner.why: Applications depend on networks to reach users, databases, APIs, and cloud services. Understanding the path helps explain both outages and security boundaries.
beginner.example: For one API request, follow the client IP, DNS result, route, firewall rule, load balancer, and destination service to find where it stops.
beginner.start: Learn IP addresses and CIDR notation first. Then calculate network ranges and trace how a packet reaches its destination.

name: Go
tagline: Go syntax, interfaces, concurrency, testing and production services.
headline: Go,
from zero to service.
blurb: Learn Go's type system, modules, errors, interfaces, generics, goroutines, channels, context, testing and profiling by building small production-shaped programs.

beginner.what: Go is a compiled programming language designed for clear, efficient software, with built-in support for concurrency and networking.
beginner.why: Its simple tooling and lightweight concurrency make it useful for command-line tools, infrastructure software, and backend services.
beginner.example: A Go service can handle many network requests with goroutines while contexts carry deadlines and cancellation through the call chain.
beginner.start: Start with packages, functions, structs, and explicit error handling, then learn goroutines and channels with cancellation.

name: Kafka
tagline: Topics, partitions, consumer groups, delivery guarantees and operations.
headline: Kafka,
event by event.
blurb: Understand the distributed log, choose partition keys, reason about offsets and rebalances, and design producers and consumers that handle retries, duplicates and schema changes safely.

beginner.what: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Producers write records to topics, and consumers read them at their own pace.
beginner.why: It lets services exchange events without requiring every receiver to be available at the exact moment an event is created.
beginner.example: An order service publishes an order-created event; billing, shipping, and analytics services can each consume it independently.
beginner.start: Learn topics, partitions, keys, offsets, and consumer groups before tuning delivery guarantees or cluster capacity.

name: Azure
tagline: Azure identity, networking, compute, data, governance and operations.
headline: Azure,
by architecture.
blurb: Learn Entra ID and RBAC, subscriptions and governance, VNets, private endpoints, compute, AKS, storage, databases, Key Vault and observability with practical decision paths.

beginner.what: Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform for compute, networking, data, identity, and managed application services.
beginner.why: It gives teams on-demand infrastructure and managed services while connecting identity, governance, and operations across an organization.
beginner.example: A web service can run in Azure, use a managed identity to read a secret, and reach a database through a private network path.
beginner.start: Understand tenants, subscriptions, resource groups, and Entra ID before exploring networking and compute services.

name: Google Cloud
tagline: GCP identity, networking, compute, data and operations.
headline: Google Cloud,
by service boundary.
blurb: Learn organizations and projects, IAM, VPC networking, Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub, Cloud Logging and cost controls with practical troubleshooting paths.

beginner.what: Google Cloud provides cloud infrastructure and managed services for applications, data processing, and machine learning.
beginner.why: Teams can scale services on demand and manage access and policy across an organization, folders, projects, and resources.
beginner.example: A workload in one project can use a service account to access a specific storage bucket in another project when IAM allows it.
beginner.start: Learn the organization, folder, project hierarchy and IAM roles, then follow one workload through its network and services.

name: Node.js
tagline: Node.js runtime, async I/O, APIs, packages, testing and operations.
headline: Node.js,
from event loop to API.
blurb: Understand the event loop, promises, streams, modules, package supply chain and production HTTP services. Practise backpressure, cancellation, tests, profiling and safe deployment.

beginner.what: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, commonly to build APIs, command-line tools, and event-driven services.
beginner.why: It lets teams use JavaScript on the server and handle many I/O operations efficiently when work is kept asynchronous and bounded.
beginner.example: An API can start several database or network requests without blocking the main event loop while waiting for each response.
beginner.start: Learn modules, promises, and the event loop, then practice building an HTTP endpoint with validation and error handling.

name: Observability & Monitoring
tagline: Prometheus, Grafana, ELK, Logstash, Kibana, Jaeger and OpenTelemetry.
headline: Observability & Monitoring
from signal to answer.
blurb: Write PromQL queries and alert rules, build Grafana dashboards, parse and route logs with Logstash, search them with Kibana KQL, and trace requests with Jaeger and OpenTelemetry.

beginner.what: Observability is the ability to understand what a system is doing by examining its outputs, especially metrics, logs, and traces.
beginner.why: When a system behaves unexpectedly, these signals help teams find what changed, where a request slowed down, and which users or services were affected.
beginner.example: A latency alert points to a slow API; a trace shows the database call taking most of the time, and related logs explain why that query slowed down.
beginner.start: Learn the difference between metrics, logs, and traces, then write a simple PromQL query and connect an alert to an actionable runbook.

name: Ansible
tagline: Playbooks, inventories, roles, safe automation and Ansible Tower/AWX.
headline: Ansible,
repeatable by design.
blurb: Write readable YAML playbooks, build reusable roles, manage secrets and inventory, test idempotence, and run governed automation through Ansible Tower / Automation Controller and AWX.

beginner.what: Ansible automates configuration and operational tasks by applying readable playbooks to selected machines or services.
beginner.why: Repeatable automation reduces manual errors and makes it easier to keep many systems configured consistently. Tower/AWX adds a managed interface for teams and scheduled jobs.
beginner.example: A playbook can ensure every web server has the right package, configuration file, and running service, while reporting which hosts changed.
beginner.start: Begin with an inventory and a read-only host listing, then write a small playbook that uses a built-in module to describe desired state.

name: Artifactory
tagline: JFrog Artifactory, Nexus, package formats and artifact supply chains.
headline: Artifacts,
promoted with trust.
blurb: Manage Maven, npm, PyPI, Docker and generic artifacts with repositories, permissions, immutable versions, retention, build metadata and promotion workflows across JFrog Artifactory and Sonatype Nexus.

beginner.what: Artifactory and similar repositories store versioned build outputs such as packages, containers, and libraries so teams can publish and retrieve them reliably.
beginner.why: A release should use known, traceable artifacts instead of rebuilding unknown files in each environment. Repositories also support access control and retention.
beginner.example: CI publishes a versioned container image once; staging and production both pull that same immutable image by digest.
beginner.start: Learn repository types, coordinates, versions, permissions, and the path from CI publication to deployment consumption.

name: Terraform
tagline: HCL, state, modules, plans, providers and safe infrastructure delivery.
headline: Terraform,
planned carefully.
blurb: Write HCL, understand providers and dependency graphs, manage remote state and locking, build reusable modules, review plans, and deliver infrastructure through secure CI workflows.

beginner.what: Terraform describes infrastructure in configuration files and compares that desired description with tracked state to plan changes.
beginner.why: Teams can review infrastructure changes before applying them, reuse modules, and recreate environments more consistently.
beginner.example: A small configuration can declare a network and a virtual machine; a plan previews what Terraform would create or change.
beginner.start: Begin with providers, resources, variables, and outputs. Learn what state records and review every plan before applying it.

name: Helm Charts
tagline: Chart structure, templates, values, releases, testing and safe upgrades.
headline: Helm charts,
packaged clearly.
blurb: Build and lint charts, write maintainable Go templates and schemas, manage values per environment, handle dependencies and secrets, and test, upgrade or roll back releases safely.

beginner.what: Helm packages and installs Kubernetes applications using charts: templates and default values that render into Kubernetes resources.
beginner.why: Charts make complex deployments reusable and configurable across environments, while releases provide a record of installations and upgrades.
beginner.example: One chart can deploy the same web service to test and production with different replica counts and resource limits supplied through values.
beginner.start: Inspect a chart's templates, values.yaml, and rendered manifests before installing it. Learn upgrades and rollback after the output makes sense.

name: Argo CD
tagline: GitOps applications, sync, health, drift, RBAC and multi-cluster delivery.
headline: Argo CD,
Git as desired state.
blurb: Model Applications and ApplicationSets, diagnose OutOfSync and degraded states, tune sync waves and health checks, secure projects and RBAC, and deliver Helm or Kustomize sources across clusters.

beginner.what: Argo CD is a GitOps delivery tool that compares Kubernetes cluster state with application configuration stored in Git and reconciles differences.
beginner.why: Git provides a reviewable source of truth for deployments, and continuous reconciliation helps teams detect and correct drift.
beginner.example: A pull request changes a replica count in Git; after approval and merge, Argo CD detects the desired change and syncs the cluster.
beginner.start: Learn repositories, Applications, sync status, health, and the difference between an out-of-sync preview and an approved sync.

name: Guitar
tagline: Guitar setup, chords, rhythm, technique and songs from first notes onward.
headline: Guitar,
one chord at a time.
blurb: Learn how the instrument works, tune it, read tabs, build chords, develop rhythm and technique, and bring each skill into songs and performance.

beginner.what: The guitar is a fretted string instrument. Pressing a string behind a fret changes its pitch; plucking or strumming makes it sound.
beginner.why: Guitar can carry melody, chords, rhythm, or accompaniment, so a few foundational skills let you play many styles and songs.
beginner.example: Tune the six strings, learn a simple chord, and keep a steady down-up strum while changing between two chords.
beginner.start: Begin with a comfortable posture, string names, tuning, and one or two open chords. Practice slowly and keep your hands relaxed.

name: Music Theory
tagline: Pitch, rhythm, scales, harmony, form and how to listen for them.
headline: Music theory,
heard and understood.
blurb: Build a practical map of sound: read rhythm, name intervals, understand keys and chords, follow musical form, and connect the terms to what you hear.

beginner.what: Music theory is a shared vocabulary for describing pitch, rhythm, melody, harmony, and musical form.
beginner.why: It helps musicians understand what they hear, communicate ideas, read music, and learn or create pieces with more confidence.
beginner.example: A major scale has a recognizable pattern of whole and half steps; naming its notes makes it easier to build melodies and chords.
beginner.start: Start with pitch names, pulse, note values, and intervals. Connect every new term to a sound you can sing or play.

name: Drums
tagline: Build time, coordination, grooves, fills and ensemble awareness.
headline: Drums,
feel the pulse.
blurb: Set up safely, develop relaxed technique, read rhythms, coordinate all four limbs, build grooves and play with a band or backing track.

beginner.what: Drums are a family of percussion instruments. A drum kit combines drums and cymbals that a player coordinates with hands and feet.
beginner.why: Drummers shape the pulse, groove, energy, and transitions that help a band play together.
beginner.example: Keep the hi-hat on steady eighth notes, play the snare on beats two and four, and add a simple kick pattern.
beginner.start: Set up the kit comfortably, protect your hearing, learn a relaxed grip, and count a steady beat before adding coordination.

name: Violin
tagline: Healthy setup, bow control, intonation, reading and expressive playing.
headline: Violin,
from open strings to songs.
blurb: Set up comfortably, make a clear sound with the bow, find notes in tune, read music, develop technique and prepare pieces for playing with others.

beginner.what: The violin is a high-pitched bowed string instrument. The left hand selects notes while the bow starts and shapes the sound.
beginner.why: Learning violin develops careful listening, fine control, musical expression, and the ability to play melody in solo or ensemble music.
beginner.example: Draw a slow, straight bow across an open string and listen for a clear, even tone from start to finish.
beginner.start: Set up the instrument without strain. Learn the open strings, a relaxed bow hold, pulse, and basic note reading before building speed.

name: Piano
tagline: Read the keyboard, coordinate both hands and make harmony come alive.
headline: Piano,
keys to music.
blurb: Find your way around the keyboard, read both staves, build scales and chords, coordinate hands, shape phrases and learn repertoire with confidence.

beginner.what: The piano is a keyboard instrument with keys that trigger hammers or electronic sounds. It can play melody and harmony at the same time.
beginner.why: The keyboard makes pitch patterns visible and gives musicians a direct way to explore scales, chords, accompaniment, and composition.
beginner.example: Find middle C, play a five-note pattern with one hand, then add a simple bass note or chord with the other.
beginner.start: Learn the groups of black keys, finger numbers, middle C, and a comfortable hand shape. Read one staff at a time and keep a steady pulse.

name: Singing & Voice
tagline: Healthy vocal technique, registers, pitch, reading and expression.
headline: Singing & voice,
with healthy technique.
blurb: Learn how the voice works, compare chest and head voice, build pitch and breath coordination, read vocal melodies and practise expression without forcing your sound.

beginner.what: Singing uses coordinated breath, vocal-fold vibration, and resonance to shape pitch and sound.
beginner.why: Voice training can build musical expression, pitch awareness, and confidence while teaching healthy, sustainable practice habits.
beginner.example: Compare a comfortable speaking-range note with a soft, higher note. Notice the different sensation without forcing either sound.
beginner.start: Begin with gentle warm-ups, comfortable notes, breath flow, and pitch matching. Stop if you feel pain or persistent strain.

name: React
tagline: Components, JSX, state, effects, forms and production patterns.
headline: React,
one component at a time.
blurb: Learn component composition, props, JSX, state, effects, forms, routing, accessibility, testing and performance through focused examples and an interactive component builder.

beginner.what: React is a JavaScript library for describing user interfaces as reusable components that respond to changing data.
beginner.why: It gives teams a consistent way to split complex screens into understandable pieces and keep the display in sync with application state.
beginner.example: A shopping page can render one ProductCard component for each product, passing each card its product details as props.
beginner.start: Begin with components, JSX, props and lists. Then learn state and events by building a small interactive counter or form.

name: SonarQube
tagline: Static analysis, quality profiles, gates, issues and CI integration.
headline: SonarQube,
quality made actionable.
blurb: Understand code analysis, rules, quality profiles, issues, quality gates, coverage, pull-request decoration and safe CI integration with practical builder exercises.

beginner.what: SonarQube analyzes source code and reports issues related to maintainability, reliability and security.
beginner.why: Shared rules and quality gates help teams catch new code risks early and track code quality over time.
beginner.example: A pull request runs analysis and receives a quality-gate status before it can be merged.
beginner.start: Learn projects, scanners, issues, quality profiles and gates. Then add a scanner step to a CI pipeline and review its first report.

name: CSS
tagline: Selectors, layouts, responsive design, visual systems and accessible UI.
headline: CSS,
style with intent.
blurb: Learn the cascade, selectors, Flexbox, Grid, responsive design, design tokens, effects and accessible states. Preview claymorphism, neumorphism and glassmorphism live.

beginner.what: CSS is the stylesheet language that controls how HTML content is presented and laid out.
beginner.why: It lets a site share consistent colors, spacing, typography and responsive layouts while keeping content separate from presentation.
beginner.example: A single .button rule can give every button the same padding, border radius and focus treatment.
beginner.start: Learn selectors, the cascade and the box model, then practice Flexbox, Grid and responsive design in the live style studio.

name: NGINX
tagline: HTTP request flow, reverse proxies, load balancing, TLS and operations.
headline: NGINX,
from request to response.
blurb: Learn how NGINX parses configuration, serves static files, proxies applications, balances upstreams, terminates TLS and exposes useful operational signals.

beginner.what: NGINX is web server software that can serve files directly and sit in front of application servers as a reverse proxy or load balancer.
beginner.why: It gives teams a controlled place to route requests, terminate TLS, cache selected responses, and spread traffic across application instances.
beginner.example: A browser requests shop.example.com; NGINX selects a matching server and location, then either returns a file or proxies the request to an application upstream.
beginner.start: Begin with the main configuration blocks and request matching. Then practise static files, reverse proxying, TLS, logs and safe reloads.

name: JavaScript
tagline: Modern JavaScript, browser APIs, asynchronous code and production tooling.
headline: JavaScript,
from values to the event loop.
blurb: Build a sturdy foundation in values, functions, objects, modules, promises, browser events, accessibility, testing and performance with runnable examples.

beginner.what: JavaScript is a programming language used in browsers and server runtimes such as Node.js. It works with values, functions, objects, modules and asynchronous operations.
beginner.why: It makes interactive websites possible and is also used for APIs, tooling and command-line applications, so one language can span much of an application stack.
beginner.example: A button click can call a function, update application state, and render a new message without reloading the page.
beginner.start: Begin with values, types, conditions, loops and functions. Then practise arrays and objects, modules, promises and browser events.
